Subject: Verbal confirmation for direct trades

Hi everyone,

Starting [date], every direct trade must be confirmed verbally before it is booked. By direct trades we mean those done bilaterally with a counterparty, not through a broker or an electronic platform.

Over the last few months we've run into several disputes about price and volume on direct deals. In each one, a short confirmation call would have caught the problem. Brokered and electronic trades come with an independent record of the terms, but direct trades do not, so getting the details right is entirely up to us.

From now on, please do the following:

1. Phone the counterparty on a recorded line to confirm the terms right after execution, and never later than 30 minutes after the trade.
2. Read back every key term: counterparty, buy/sell, product, volume, price, delivery point or settlement terms, and start and end dates.
3. Write the name of the person you spoke to and the time of the call on the deal ticket.
4. If any term does not match, do not book the trade yet, and escalate immediately to [Name] in middle office.

This step comes on top of the written confirmation process and does not replace it. The confirmations group will keep sending written confirms as usual.

I realize this adds a minute or two to each deal. That is still much less time than we have spent untangling disputes afterward, and it protects us as well as our counterparties.

If you have questions or spot practical problems with the process, please send them to me by [date] so we can resolve them before it starts.

Thank you,
[Your Name]

A quick note before the list: Mariya Takeuchi made her debut in 1978, so she does belong to the late-70s scene, but most of her best-known songs date from the 1980s onward. Her career has run for more than forty years, and her signature sound is at the heart of what is now called "city pop." The songs below span her entire career, and the 1970s material is labeled so you can concentrate on it if your assignment calls for that.

## Late 1970s – Early 1980s (RCA years)

**"Modotte Oide, Watashi no Jikan" (1978)**
This was her debut single, a light, polished pop song that introduced her as a college-aged singer with a clear, warm voice. It isn't her biggest hit, but it matters as the beginning of her career.

**"September" (1979)**
One of her signature early songs, written by Takao Kisugi with lyrics by Takashi Matsumoto. It's a bittersweet song about a relationship fading as summer gives way to autumn. It brought her wide recognition and is still a fan favorite.

**"Watashi no Heart wa Stop Motion" (1979)**
This upbeat single was used in a cosmetics commercial, which helped make her a household name. It shows the bright, idol-like side of her early image.

**"Fushigi na Peach Pie" (1980)**
This is probably her biggest hit from the RCA era. It was also linked to a cosmetics campaign, and it's playful and catchy, with a sunny pop arrangement. If you need a single song to stand for her earliest fame, it's a strong pick.

**"Sweetest Music" (1980)**
Taken from the album *Miss M*, which was partly recorded in Los Angeles with American session musicians. The song shows how closely her sound was tied to West Coast AOR at that time.

## Mid-1980s (after her marriage to Tatsuro Yamashita)

She married the musician and producer Tatsuro Yamashita in 1982, stepped away from performing, and came back as a songwriter who wrote most of her own material. Yamashita produced and arranged much of her later work.

**"Plastic Love" (1984)**
From the album *Variety*. It is now her most famous song around the world. It did only modestly well when it came out, but around 2017 an unofficial YouTube upload went viral, and the song became the face of the global city pop revival. Its funky bassline, disco-tinged groove and lonely lyrics about a woman who hides her heartbreak in nightlife have been covered and remixed endlessly.

**"Mou Ichido" (1984)**
Another single from *Variety*, this mid-tempo ballad displayed her growing strength as a songwriter.

**"Genki wo Dashite" (1984 / 1987)**
She first wrote it for the actress and singer Hiroko Yakushimaru, then recorded her own version for the album *Request* (1987). It's a gentle, encouraging song that tells a friend to cheer up after a breakup, and in Japan it is one of her most beloved tracks.

## Late 1980s – 1990s

**"Single Again" (1989)**
A dramatic ballad about meeting a former lover after both people's lives have changed. It served as a TV drama theme and became one of her biggest commercial hits.

**"Kokuhaku" (1990)**
Another ballad tied to a drama, emotionally heavy and very popular, which carried on her success with mature love songs.

**"Junai Rhapsody" (1994)**
A major hit that appeared on the compilation *Impressions*, which sold several million copies and ranks among the best-selling albums in Japanese history.

**"Camouflage" (1998)**
Used as a TV drama theme, this song reached the top of the Oricon charts and proved she was still commercially strong two decades after her debut.

## 2000s and Later

**"Inochi no Uta" (2008 / 2012)**
Originally written under a pen name for an NHK drama, this song about gratitude for life later became widely known through her own recording and is often sung at ceremonies in Japan.

**Recent albums**
*Denim* (2007), *Trad* (2014) and *Precious Days* (2024) show that she has kept putting out new material, even though she rarely tours.

## Suggestions for Your Assignment

- If your focus is strictly the 1970s, use "Modotte Oide, Watashi no Jikan," "September" and "Watashi no Heart wa Stop Motion," and mention "Fushigi na Peach Pie" as the 1980 high point of that period.
- If your focus is her overall popularity, "Plastic Love," "Single Again" and "Genki wo Dashite" are essential.
- If your focus is cultural impact, "Plastic Love" is the key case study, because its rediscovery online is a good example of how the internet revived interest in older Japanese pop among international audiences.

Since release years and chart details sometimes differ from source to source, it's worth checking specific dates against an official discography or the Oricon database before you cite them.

Dr. Peter Albright broke the news the way some men hand out parking tickets: crisply, and with a faint suggestion that he was doing her a favor.

"Six months," he said. "Maybe less. I'd put your affairs in order, Mrs. Kowalczyk."

Edna Kowalczyk was eighty-one. She had buried a husband, two dogs and a forty-year attachment to menthol cigarettes. She glanced down at Dr. Albright's loafers, which had tassels, and decided on the spot that she would not give him the satisfaction.

"I'll see you in six months," she said.

"I hope so," he answered, already reaching for the next chart.

At home she wrote a list. It wasn't a list of affairs to be put in order. Its title was THINGS ALBRIGHT WILL HAVE TO HEAR ABOUT, and item one was *Walk to the mailbox without the cane.*

That took three weeks. Her hip complained the whole time, and she told it, out loud, that it could take its complaints to Dr. Albright.

Item two was the county fair, where she meant to enter her rhubarb pie for the first time since 1997. Item three was learning the tablet her granddaughter had given her, since she had heard that you could post reviews of doctors on the internet.

At the six-month appointment, Dr. Albright frowned at her bloodwork for a very long time.

"Well," he said. "This is unusual."

"Second place," Edna said. "For the pie. The woman who won is married to one of the judges. I'm appealing."

He had no idea how to respond to that, so he told her to return in three months.

She returned in three months, and again three months after that. Her granddaughter, Talia, began driving her to the appointments because she wanted to watch. Edna would sit ramrod straight on the crinkly paper, Dr. Albright would examine her numbers as if they had insulted him personally, and Talia would bite the inside of her cheek to keep from laughing.

"What's your secret?" a nurse once asked her in the hallway.

"Pettiness," Edna said. "Wildly underrated."

That wasn't the full story. There was also the pie, which won first place the next year, once the judge's wife retired. There was the tablet, where she found out that Talia had been posting photos of her with captions like *my grandma is undefeated*. There was the spring she planted tomatoes she had no business expecting to eat, and ate them anyway, warm from the vine, with a little salt.

But spite was what had pulled her out of the chair that first morning, and Edna believed in giving credit where it was due.

Four years after the six-month prognosis, Dr. Albright announced that he was retiring. Edna sent a card. Inside, in careful cursive, she wrote: *Congratulations. I'll be here when you get back.*

Talia asked if that was a little mean.

"Sweetheart," Edna said, cutting her a slice of pie, "it's a lot mean. That's the whole point."
